# AI Agent-Assisted MicroDuck Walking Training: From Task Description to Policy

NVIDIA demonstrated a process that starts with a task description, creates obstacle scenarios, trains, and validates the MicroDuck motion policy. This section breaks down each step, and the publicly available Isaac Lab walking task explains how to get started. The following command comes from a public tutorial, but this repository has not completed training and validation for this version yet.

## How the demonstration works

[NVIDIA navigation simulation](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/using-ai-agents-to-teach-robots-like-microduck-to-walk-in-simulation) The task description provided aims to "build and test the Microduck simulation obstacle field with navigation and motion challenges". The original text presents the example prompt with ellipses, along with its research plan, concept diagram, asset list, handover, modeling, and validation steps. The full presentation can be found in the first section of the original text.

1. **Planning**: Hermes and Nemotron 3.5 Bolt organize robot data, routes, dimensions, scene lists, and handover materials.
2. **Modeling and Assembly**: Astra uses FreeCAD and Blender to create assets, and then assembles scenes in Isaac Sim. Simulation assets can also come from [SimReady Central](https://huggingface.co/blog/nvidia/simready-central-assets-robotics-ai-factories).
3. **Training**: Starting with the MicroDuck example environment in Isaac Lab and pre-trained walking policies, further train obstacle movement policies that incorporate depth cameras and robot state observations. NVIDIA indicates that this adaptation experiment uses a RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition with 4096 parallel environments.
4. **Evaluation and Deployment Preparation**: Place the trained policy back into Isaac Sim to check performance in obstacle crossing, falling, and collision scenarios; then prepare for migration to a real robot through actuator models and randomization.

The agent organizes tasks and calls tools; the policy is updated based on observations, actions, rewards, and reinforcement learning in simulation. The NVIDIA page provides the process and entry points for basic tasks; however, whether the complete assets for obstacle scenarios, training configurations, and the weights of this visual policy are publicly available has not been verified, and a complete release package that can be reproduced is still unavailable.

## Open Source Baseline: Isaac Lab Walk

[NVIDIA and Hugging Face's Microduck training tutorial ](https://huggingface.co/blog/nvidia/microduck-isaac-lab-sim-to-real) provides tasks for walking on flat and rough surfaces. Here, [Isaac Lab's fixed submission 0c10609 ](https://github.com/isaac-sim/IsaacLab/tree/0c10609fd76534ccee3ae3973625003d65085441) is used as a code reference, and the [ task registration ](https://github.com/isaac-sim/IsaacLab/blob/0c10609fd76534ccee3ae3973625003d65085441/source/isaaclab_tasks/isaaclab_tasks/contrib/microduck/__init__.py) includes two tasks: Flat and Rough. The upstream repository uses the BSD-3-Clause license. This is a link to the upstream code; its implementation is not copied.

The rough baseline includes slopes, steps, and random terrain; the current code indicates it is a visual-free speed walking task, and the foot height ray does not enter the actor observation. Therefore, it is suitable for reproduction of walking training but cannot be directly used as a depth vision obstacle avoidance policy in NVIDIA demonstrations. For flat and rough ground tasks, a 61-dimensional policy observation and a 14-dimensional joint target action are used; when publishing the policy, the observation order, normalization, and action scaling also need to be aligned.

### Environment and Training

Requires Linux, supported NVIDIA GPU and drivers, Git, and uv. The specific versions and hardware requirements are subject to [Isaac Lab installation documentation ](https://isaac-sim.github.io/IsaacLab/main/source/setup/installation/index.html). The following are the steps for using a fixed source code version in an independent working directory:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/isaac-sim/IsaacLab.git
cd IsaacLab
git checkout 0c10609fd76534ccee3ae3973625003d65085441
uv sync
uv run isaaclab list_envs --keyword MicroDuck --show_presets
```

The list should include Flat and Rough tasks; when the tasks are not found, check the code version and dependency installation first. Start the rough ground training according to the upstream tutorial:

```bash
uv run isaaclab train \
  --rl_library rsl_rl \
  --task IsaacContrib-Velocity-Rough-MicroDuck \
  --num_envs 4096 \
  presets=backlash
```

`presets=backlash` enables the actuator configuration with mechanical clearance; dynamic parameters are also randomized during training. 4096 is the number of parallel environments for the upstream tutorial, which should be adjusted according to the memory available; the training time and performance after reducing the number of parallel environments need to be measured again. The specific paths for the training logs and checkpoints depend on the running output.

### Playback and Export

After the training generates a checkpoint, use the upstream playback command in an environment with a graphical display:

```bash
uv run isaaclab play \
  --rl_library rsl_rl \
  --task IsaacContrib-Velocity-Rough-MicroDuck \
  --checkpoint latest \
  --num_envs 16 \
  --viz newton_gl \
  presets=backlash
```

When replaying the upstream tutorial instructions, `exported/` used in that run will generate `policy.pt` and `policy.onnx`. Check the output to see if balance is maintained and the speed command is followed; record the number of falls, speed errors, performance on different terrains, and the video. For real robot ONNX deployment, a matching onboard interface must be used, and refer to [ Microduck deployment guide ](https://huggingface.co/blog/nvidia/microduck-isaac-lab-sim-to-real#6-deploy-the-onnx-locomotion-policy-on-a-real-microduck).

## Connection with existing content in this topic

This topic already includes [MuJoCo walking HelloWorld](../../../../../16-专题组队学习/05-MicroDuck运动策略与任务开发专题/03-Notebook/00_MuJoCo策略控制_HelloWorld.ipynb), [basketball balance](../01-microduck-basketball-balance-reinforcement-learning/README.md), and multiple task training. First, use HelloWorld to understand the process of “observation → policy → joint goal → physics update”, then read the task configurations in the Isaac Lab environment, which allows you to compare the observation, action, reward, and executor models of the two simulation training stacks. Visual obstacle avoidance requires additional camera observations, task definition, training configuration, and verifiable evaluation—it cannot be simply replaced by a single text instruction.
